solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Chatter about actors running popular stall

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so the word for chatter is wrapped round the rest

parts.note: to prate is to chatter idly

indicators.note: things that are running are in motion, so the actors are set moving into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
what is popular is in fashion

explanation.surface: A gossiping crowd of performers hanging round a well-liked market stall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stall' looks like a noun for a market booth, but it is the verb meaning to play for time.
explanation.definitionFit: To procrastinate is to delay action deliberately, which is what someone stalling does.

clue.text: Manuscript of drivel Treasury half-spun

indicators.note: only half of the word is kept, the other half being thrown away

parts.note: pap is worthless, insipid talk or writing

indicators.note: something spun round faces the other way, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: the back half of the eight-letter word

explanation.surface: A government document full of nonsense, with the Treasury's part only half done.
explanation.walkthrough: The last four letters of Treasury, turned round, follow PAP to make PAPYRUS.
explanation.definitionFit: A papyrus is an ancient handwritten document on reed paper, a kind of manuscript.

clue.text: Ill-prepared angler may be so impudent

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a fisherman who has come without the cord for the rod
second meaning: behaving improperly or cheekily

explanation.surface: An angler who turned up unready might be cheeky too.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is read literally: an angler lacking fishing line is without it.
explanation.definitionFit: Being out of line is an idiom for speaking or acting improperly, which is what impudent behaviour is.

clue.text: River perfect following closure of pier

indicators.note: the closure of a word is its end, so only its final letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of pier
to hone is to perfect a skill

explanation.surface: A river looking its best once the pier has shut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' places HONE after R; in a down answer that means beneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhone is a major river flowing from Switzerland through France.

clue.text: Outlines singular vessels with two masts

parts.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
a ketch is a two-masted sailing boat

explanation.surface: Describing the shape of some unusual two-masted boats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singular' reads as 'remarkable', but it is just the abbreviation S.
explanation.definitionFit: Sketches are rough drawings or summaries, so as a verb it means to give the outline of something.

clue.text: Two fishes not doing an awful lot

parts.note: the id is a variant spelling of the ide, a freshwater fish
the ling is a long sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A couple of fish lazing about, barely moving.
explanation.walkthrough: The ide is also spelt ID in Chambers, a dictionary crossword setters lean on for short variants.
explanation.definitionFit: Idling means passing time without work or activity, so doing very little.

clue.text: South American male unmarried soldier hugs

indicators.note: to hug is to hold in the arms, so the soldier wraps round the other word
M is the usual abbreviation for married, so being unmarried strips that letter out

parts.note: a marine is a soldier serving at sea
a gent is a man

explanation.surface: A bachelor soldier from South America embracing someone.
explanation.walkthrough: MARINE loses M (married) to leave ARINE, which then hugs GENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Argentine is an adjective or noun for someone or something from Argentina, a South American country.

clue.text: Sees terrorists securing compound

indicators.note: securing means holding fast, so the phrase keeps the answer locked inside it

parts.note: sitting across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone notices militants guarding a walled compound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Compound' looks like a fortified enclosure, but here it is a chemical compound.
explanation.definitionFit: An ester is an organic chemical compound formed from an acid and an alcohol.

clue.text: City of Bergen periodically crowning queens?

indicators.note: periodically means at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: first, third and fifth letters
queen is slang for a gay man, so the question mark flags these queens as men

explanation.surface: A Norwegian city now and then crowning royal women.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, crowning means sitting on top. 'Of Bergen' tempts a Norwegian place; the answer is a German city.
explanation.definitionFit: Bremen is a port city in northern Germany.

clue.text: Spooner's very warm staff explore underground

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of two words

parts.note: very warm is hot and a staff is a pole; swap their opening sounds

explanation.surface: A hot stick taken caving.
explanation.definitionFit: To pothole is to explore caves and shafts, the British sport of caving.

clue.text: Ignition device probably easier to carry

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a gadget for making a flame

explanation.surface: A cigarette lighter is handy because it slips into a pocket.
explanation.definitionFit: Lighter names both a device that lights things and the comparative of light, meaning less heavy.

clue.text: Item maybe loaded back inside barrel first

indicators.note: back means going backwards, so the concealed letters read right to left
inside says the letters lie within the following words

parts.note: sitting across the two words, read forwards

explanation.surface: Gunpowder goes in the barrel first when loading an old weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barrel' looks like part of the gun, but it simply holds the letters, read in reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: A rifle is a firearm, an example of something that may be loaded with ammunition.

clue.text: Sister feeds swimmer with drink problem

indicators.note: feeding something puts food into it, so the sister goes inside

parts.note: a fish is a swimmer
a nun is a religious sister
taken as a spirit

explanation.surface: A nun nourishing someone who has an alcohol problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink problem' reads as one phrase; split it: drink is RUM and problem is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A conundrum is a puzzling question or difficulty, so a problem.

clue.text: Shallow ooze encircling class

indicators.note: encircling means surrounding, so the ooze goes round the word for class

parts.note: to seep is to ooze slowly
a kind is a class or sort

explanation.surface: Mud that surrounds a group of things is not very deep.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin-deep means superficial, only on the surface, which is what shallow means of feelings or character.

clue.text: Strip books bound by gloomy European

indicators.note: something bound by another is held within it

parts.note: dismal means gloomy
NT is the New Testament, a set of books
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A depressed European stripping books of their bindings.
explanation.walkthrough: NT, the New Testament, is the usual crossword shorthand for books.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismantle is to take apart, as when you strip down an engine.

clue.text: Maiden driving out having day off

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or not right, so the letters are put into a new order
D stands for day, and having it off removes it from the word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A young woman out for a drive on her day off work.
explanation.walkthrough: DRIVING loses D for day, and the remaining six letters rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A maiden is an unmarried girl, traditionally one who is a virgin, so the words are synonyms.

clue.text: Pet possibly destroyed tea garden

indicators.note: something destroyed is wrecked, so the following letters are broken up and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A family pet has torn up the café garden.
explanation.definitionFit: A Great Dane is a large breed of dog, an example of a pet, hence 'possibly'.

clue.text: Italian with starter of mint in a little soup

parts.note: con is the Italian word for with

indicators.note: in says one letter goes inside the word for a little

parts.note: some means a small quantity

indicators.note: the starter of a meal comes first, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: first letter of mint

explanation.surface: An Italian adds a hint of mint to a small bowl of soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italian with' looks like an Italian person accompanying something; it is the Italian word for with. M goes inside SOME.
explanation.definitionFit: Consommé is a clear soup made from concentrated meat or fish stock.

clue.text: A number cycling over still

indicators.note: cycling round moves the first letter to the back of the word

parts.note: seven is a number
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Riding a bike past a figure that stays motionless.
explanation.walkthrough: SEVEN with its S moved to the end gives EVENS, then O.
explanation.definitionFit: Even so and still both mean nevertheless, as in 'it was raining; still, we went'.

clue.text: Take off from base on small coastal area

parts.note: e is the base of natural logarithms
S is the abbreviation for small
a cape is a headland on the coast

explanation.surface: An aircraft leaves a small seaside airbase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts the following pieces after E. E as base comes from mathematics.
explanation.definitionFit: To take off can mean to leave in a hurry or run away, a synonym for escape.

clue.text: Solitary man interrupting poor Charlie

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break in, so these letters go into the middle of the other word

parts.note: poor quality is bad
a solitary thing is just one
he refers to a man

explanation.surface: A lonely man barging in on a hard-up fellow called Charlie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' looks like a name; in British slang a charlie is a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonehead is a stupid person, just as a charlie is British slang for a fool.

clue.text: Excavated around New Age prison

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the excavated word goes round the next letter

parts.note: dug is past tense of dig
N is the abbreviation for new
an eon is an age

explanation.surface: A modern jail dug out of the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: A dungeon is an underground cell in a castle, a kind of prison.

clue.text: Tin of rolled meat stuffed with game

indicators.note: rolling something over turns it the other way, so the letters run backwards
something stuffed has filling put inside it, so the game goes inside the meat

parts.note: ham is cured pork
loo is an old card game

explanation.surface: A can of meat roll with game filling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tin' looks like a can for the meat; it is old British slang for money. Loo is a card game once popular in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Moolah and tin are both slang words for money.

clue.text: Birds from coast Cook cooked

indicators.note: cooked can mean falsified or doctored, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Captain Cook cooked the birds he found on the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain James Cook charted the Australian coast, where cockatoos live, which is the joke of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Cockatoos are crested parrots native to Australasia, so they are birds.

clue.text: Two-thirds of delicacy left? Complain!

indicators.note: only two-thirds of the word survives, so its final third is dropped

parts.note: caviar is a luxury food of fish roe
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A diner grumbles that most of the delicacy was left uneaten.
explanation.walkthrough: CAVIAR loses its last two letters to leave CAVI, then L.
explanation.definitionFit: To cavil is to raise petty objections, a way of complaining.

clue.text: Giant winged creature eviscerated Aladdin

parts.note: a tit is a small bird

indicators.note: an eviscerated body has had its insides removed, leaving only the outer shell

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: A huge flying beast tore Aladdin apart.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titans were a race of giants in Greek myth, and a titan is anyone of great size.

clue.text: Places to read south of tense capital

parts.note: T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense
unis, short for universities, are places to read a subject

explanation.surface: Libraries found in the south of a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English you read a subject at university. 'South of' places UNIS under T in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunis is the capital city of Tunisia.

clue.text: A lot changed after bigwig turned key

indicators.note: turned round means facing back, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: a very important person

indicators.note: changed means altered, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Much changed once an important person turned a key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' looks like a noun for a lock; here it is the adjective meaning crucial.
explanation.definitionFit: Pivotal means of central importance, which is what key means as an adjective.

clue.text: Composite image of Mike acting without son?

parts.note: Mike is M in the radio alphabet

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the letter for son is taken away

parts.note: an actor at work is on stage
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A photo collage of Mike performing, minus his boy.
explanation.definitionFit: A montage is a picture made by combining several images, so a composite image.

clue.text: Country Tale chapter 10 by Gertrude or Rick?

parts.note: a tale can be a falsehood
CH is the abbreviation for chapter
the number written as a word
Gertrude Stein was an American writer; Rick Stein is a British TV chef

explanation.surface: Chapter ten of a country story, written by Gertrude or Rick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tale chapter 10' reads like a reference in a book, but each word is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Liechtenstein is a small principality in the Alps between Switzerland and Austria.
